vignette:
She is seventy-four years old, though her back tells her she is older. Every morning before the sun breaches the horizon, she rises from the thin mattress she shares with Joseph, her partner of forty years. Her body moves by memory: pulling on a faded cotton dress, tying a scarf over her gray hair, stepping into rubber boots caked with dry red soil. She has worked this land since she was a girl—first alongside her mother, then for white farmers, and now tending her own small plot of maize and beans behind the compound. The work is the one thing that has never betrayed her.

But the memories have found her even here.

It happened when she was twenty-three, walking home from the market along the path that cut through the tall grass. The man was someone she knew by sight, a farmer from the next village. He stepped out from behind the acacia tree and grabbed her arm. She remembers the smell of his sweat, the feel of his calloused hand over her mouth, the sound of her own voice trapped in her throat. Afterward, she lay in the dust until the moon rose. She never told anyone—not her mother, not the village elder, not Joseph when he courted her a year later. She washed herself in the river and buried the story deep.

But the story has claws.

Now, when she bends over the maize stalks, the scent of damp earth and sweat can pull her back. Her hands freeze. Her heart beats against her ribs like a trapped bird. She has to crouch there, gripping a hoe, until the world returns. Joseph thinks she is just tired. He touches her shoulder at night, and sometimes she flinches before she can stop herself. She sees the hurt flicker across his face, but she cannot explain. The words have never come.

She has learned to avoid certain things without knowing why she avoids them. She will not walk the old path to the market, even though it is shorter. She makes a wide detour through the church compound instead. She does not attend the annual harvest festival where men drink palm wine and laugh loudly. She avoids the neighbor who smells like the man—a sharp, sour scent she cannot name. Joseph grumbles that she has become “difficult,” that she stays too close to home. She says nothing.

At night, the dreams come. She is twenty-three again, walking through grass that reaches her waist. The man’s hand covers her mouth, and she cannot scream. She wakes gasping, drenched in sweat, Joseph’s arm draped over her hip. She lies still, staring at the crack in the ceiling, counting the breaths until dawn.

She still goes to the fields. The soil is the only thing she can trust. She plants, she weeds, she harvests. But the world feels thinner now, as if a veil separates her from everyone else. She watches other women laugh and gossip at the watering hole, and she feels nothing. Joseph tells her she is distant, but she cannot reach across the distance. She is seventy-four years old, and the girl on the path has never left her.
